lines: The oven, two big decks of it, ticking as it warms. Most mornings it's scones and muffins for the case out front, and the whole kitchen smells of them.
There's a timer on a string hung on the hook beside it. Somebody's never once needed it.
Steel work tables all along the wall: the big stand mixer, a scale that weighs to the gram, and a bench scraper worn smooth from years of good use.
This is where the coffee shop's own baking gets done — the scones, the cookies, whatever goes in the case each morning.
Two fridges and a chest freezer, humming in three different keys: butter by the case, eggs by the flat, milk and cream for the espresso machine out front.
Everything in here is going to be breakfast for somebody by the end of the week.
A table kept clear at the end of the room, with a turntable and a rack of food colours on the shelf above it.
Some nights a baker borrows the kitchen after the shop's locked up and builds her custom cakes here. Most days it's just where the trays get stacked.
A rolling rack of trays, cooling: lemon shortbread cookies, every tray of them. They go out front by the dozen and they're gone.
Buttery, a little sharp, sugar on top. One is never the number.
